headline: Tribunal investigation reveals weapons on RAB helicopter during July uprising
summary: A tribunal's investigation into the July mass uprising has uncovered details about the types of weapons and ammunition loaded onto a RAB helicopter. This development sheds light on the events of the tumultuous period.
details: A tribunal investigating the July mass uprising has uncovered specific details concerning the weapons and ammunition that were loaded onto a Rapid Action Battalion (RAB) helicopter. This information is a crucial part of the ongoing inquiry into the events of that tumultuous period.

The investigation aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the actions taken during the uprising. Further findings are expected as the tribunal continues its work to establish the full sequence of events.

headline_marked: [[Nearly 9 in 10 families borrowed money]] due to measles outbreak in Bangladesh: Assessment
headline: Nearly 9 in 10 families borrowed money due to measles outbreak in Bangladesh: Assessment
summary: A new assessment by BDRCS and IFRC reveals the devastating financial toll of the ongoing measles outbreak, with most families exhausting savings or taking loans to cover treatment costs.
details: The ongoing measles outbreak has inflicted a devastating financial toll on affected families in Bangladesh. A new assessment reveals that nearly nine in 10 households had to borrow money, and six in 10 exhausted their savings to cover treatment-related costs.

Conducted by the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS) and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the assessment highlights that the economic burden extends far beyond hospital care, despite free treatment at government facilities.

The findings are based on a survey of 2,746 measles-affected households whose members received treatment at 12 government medical college and district hospitals between May and June. Out of these, 2,442 households, or 88.9 percent, reported borrowing money for expenses.

Beyond borrowing, 1,670 households (60.8 percent) depleted their savings, while 112 households (4.1 percent) resorted to selling assets. Another 90 households (3.3 percent) relied on donations to manage the financial strain.

Nazma Begum's family from Shariatpur is one such example, pushed into debt after her 10-month-old daughter, Ashya, contracted measles. Ashya received treatment at the DNCC Dedicated Covid-19 Hospital in Dhaka, now exclusively treating measles patients.

Nazma's husband, a mason, faces irregular work, forcing them to take a loan to bring their daughter to Dhaka for treatment after local facilities referred her. This illustrates a common challenge for many low-income families.

The country is grappling with an unprecedented outbreak, with at least 1.44 lakh patients, mostly children, hospitalized with measles or measles-like symptoms. As of July 31, the measles-related death toll stood at 810.

Many families are compelled to travel to the capital after local health facilities struggle to manage complications. A significant number reported having already exhausted their savings treating other illnesses before measles struck their children.

For low-income families, the health crisis quickly escalates into a financial one. To afford treatment in Dhaka, many borrow from relatives, neighbours, or informal lenders to cover essential costs like ambulance fares, medicines, tests, and food.

Despite free treatment at government hospitals, related expenses typically range between Tk 20,000 and Tk 40,000. For children requiring intensive care at private hospitals, costs can soar into several lakh taka.

The burden is compounded by lost wages or income sources while caring for sick children in hospitals, particularly for the 78 percent of affected families working in the informal sector. Treatment and related expenses can average Tk 16,000 and go up to Tk 65,000, including transport and diagnostics.
